text: Arrow functions and destructuring are two of the most-used pieces of modern JavaScript syntax — once they're comfortable, most real code reads noticeably faster, and nearly every blockchain library's own documentation examples lean on both constantly.

An arrow function is shorter to write than a regular function, and with a single expression body and no curly braces at all, the return is implicit — whatever that one expression evaluates to is automatically returned, with no return keyword written anywhere. This compact form is everywhere in real code, especially whenever a small function is passed directly as an argument into another function.

Here's the real difference, not just the shorter syntax: arrow functions don't have their own this, they inherit it lexically from whatever scope they're written inside, at the moment they're defined. Regular functions get their own this, which depends entirely on how they're called and frequently isn't what you expect inside a callback — that unpredictability is the actual reason arrow functions are preferred there, not just that they save a few keystrokes.

Array destructuring pulls values out of an array into named variables, by position, in a single line — instead of writing coords bracket zero, coords bracket one, coords bracket two as three separate statements. You can even skip an element you don't need entirely by leaving an empty slot in the pattern.

Object destructuring pulls properties out by name instead of position. You can rename a property while pulling it out if the default name would clash with something else, and supply a default value that only kicks in if that property is missing or explicitly undefined on the object.

You're ready for lesson ten when you can destructure two named properties out of an object in one line, and explain why an arrow function is the safer choice inside a class method's callback. Arrow functions for shorter syntax and predictable this, destructuring for pulling values out of arrays and objects in one line. Next up: template literals — building strings the way real code actually does it.
